lessons.title: Heap Concept and Properties
lessons.concept: A heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the heap property. In a max-heap, every parent node is greater than or equal to its children; in a min-heap, every parent node is less than or equal to its children. The root always holds the maximum (max-heap) or minimum (min-heap).
lessons.formula: Complete binary tree: all levels filled except possibly last, filled left to right. Max-heap: parent >= children. Min-heap: parent <= children. Array indexing (0-based): parent(i)=(i-1)//2, left(i)=2*i+1, right(i)=2*i+2.
lessons.worked_example: Array [10, 7, 9, 3, 5] represents a max-heap: 10 at root, children 7 and 9, and 3,5 under 7. Root 10 is the maximum element.
mistakes: Confusing heap with a fully sorted structure (heap is partially ordered)
Assuming left child is always smaller than right child in a max-heap
Forgetting the complete binary tree requirement

lessons.title: Heap Operations: Insert and Extract
lessons.concept: Insertion adds a new element at the end (to maintain completeness) and then heapifies up (bubble up) to restore heap property. Extracting the root removes the top element, moves the last element to root, and heapifies down (sift down) to restore order.
lessons.formula: Insert: append -> while node > parent (max-heap) swap up. Extract-max: save root, move last to root, reduce size, while node < larger child swap down. Time: O(log n) per operation.
mistakes: Heapifying in the wrong direction (up vs down) for the operation
Not comparing with the correct child during sift down (use larger child in max-heap)
Breaking completeness by inserting at an arbitrary position
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Heap Applications and Complexity
lessons.concept: Heaps efficiently support priority queue operations, where the highest (or lowest) priority element is accessed quickly. Common uses include heap sort, finding k largest/smallest elements, and algorithms like Dijkstra/Prim (conceptually with priority queues).
lessons.formula: Peek root: O(1). Insert/extract: O(log n). Build heap: O(n). Heap sort: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra (in-place array heap) or O(n) if counting output separately.
lessons.worked_example: To get the 3 largest elements from a stream, a min-heap of size 3 can keep candidates: push elements and if size > 3 pop the minimum, leaving the 3 largest.
mistakes: Using a max-heap when a min-heap is needed for k-largest maintenance (or vice versa)
Assuming heap provides sorted iteration order without repeated extracts
Confusing build-heap complexity O(n) with repeated insertion O(n log n)

practice.question: In a max-heap, which element is always at the root?
practice.explanation: By the max-heap property, every parent is >= its children, so the maximum element resides at the root.

practice.question: What is the time complexity of inserting an element into a binary heap of n elements?
practice.explanation: Insertion appends at the end and may bubble up along the height of the heap; height of a complete binary tree is O(log n).

practice.explanation: For 0-based indexing, left child is 2*i + 1, right child is 2*i + 2, and parent is (i-1)//2.

questions.question: In a min-heap, the relationship between a parent node and its children is:
questions.explanation: In a min-heap, each parent node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the minimum element is at the root.

questions.explanation: The maximum element in a max-heap is at the root, so peeking/reading it takes constant time O(1).

questions.question: After removing the root from a heap, which step restores the heap property?

options.B: Move last element to root and heapify down

questions.explanation: Extract-root replaces the root with the last element to keep the tree complete, then sifts it down (heapify down) to restore the heap property.

questions.question: Which statement about a heap is TRUE?

options.A: A heap is always fully sorted like a sorted array
options.B: A heap is a complete binary tree with heap-order property
options.C: In a max-heap, every left child is greater than right child
options.D: Heaps cannot be stored in arrays

questions.explanation: Heaps are complete binary trees satisfying heap order; they are partially ordered, not fully sorted, and can be efficiently stored in arrays.

questions.question: Heap sort has a typical time complexity of:
questions.explanation: Heap sort builds a heap and performs n extract operations, each taking O(log n), resulting in O(n log n) overall time.
